name: Benzoyl peroxide wash for body odor
lead: Benzoyl peroxide is an oxidizer used mainly as an acne medication. It is sold over the counter and appears on the WHO list of essential medicines.[1] In looksmaxxing and body-care discussions, benzoyl peroxide washes are applied to the armpits or body on the theory that they kill odor-producing bacteria.

Wikipedia's article does not mention body odor. For acne, the compound is thought to kill Cutibacterium acnes through oxidative damage, reduce sebum and unclog pores.[1] No studies of benzoyl peroxide for underarm odor were found.

paras: The medication is mainly used for acne, alone or combined with antibiotics, salicylic acid, sulfur or adapalene.[1] Non-medical uses include bleaching and polymerization in plastics manufacture.[1]

Proponents say that because the compound kills skin bacteria, it also reduces the bacteria that turn apocrine sweat into odor. The body odor article describes that bacterial mechanism and lists antibacterial washes among treatments, but does not mention benzoyl peroxide.[2]

Skin irritation including redness, burning and dryness is common and dose-dependent.[1] About 1 in 500 people have a hypersensitivity reaction, and roughly a third of users experience phototoxicity under UVB light, so sunscreen is advised.[1] Contact with fabric or hair can cause permanent color fading, including indirect contact such as via a towel.[1]
Brodie first prepared the compound in 1858; skin uses were reported from around 1905, it was proposed for acne in 1934, and the US approved it for acne in 1960.[1]
No studies found for body odor.

timeline.event: Benjamin Collins Brodie first prepares benzoyl peroxide.[1]

card.summary: Acne antibacterial wash repurposed for pit odor; the mechanism is plausible but odor use is untested.
card.note: Irritation, photosensitivity and permanent fabric bleaching.

quick.overview:
Benzoyl peroxide washes are acne products that some people use on the armpits to reduce odor.

Wikipedia does not mention body odor use, and no studies were found testing it.
quick.mechanism: For acne it kills bacteria by oxidative damage; proponents extend this to odor bacteria.
quick.risks: Irritation is common, about 1 in 500 have hypersensitivity, phototoxicity occurs, and it can permanently bleach fabrics and towels.
